gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the 0.01 mm rapid-trigger figure is a firmware setting that only holds after the board's per-key travel calibration, and that the Gamakay x NaughShark NS68 puts that calibration and adjustable top and bottom dead zones (down to 0.0 mm) in a browser driver, as Moussa Obscur of TechXReviews described.
standout_why: Compared against six pages I opened. mechanicalkeyboard.net (2026-11-10) already tells readers to run the driver's calibration flow, and that magnet polarity matters when swapping switches. gamepadsquire.com (2026-08-09) already says HE68 Lite double-registration is 'usually resolved by recalibrating the board', and that the AULA F75 HE's 8K is wired-only. setupinsider.com and keyboardverdict.com define rapid trigger as reset-on-lift but say nothing on dead zones or calibration. None of them mentions dead zones, and none covers the NS68's calibration or dead-zone controls. The two cited pages (PC Gamer's Hall effect guide and RTINGS' rapid trigger research) returned only navigation to my fetcher, so I could not compare against their body text. That, plus the finding resting on a reviewer and not on Gamakay's own page (HTTP 429 on all five tries), keeps this at 1.
decides: It confirms the pick but does not change it. The NS68 Wired has the controls that make a 0.01 mm rapid-trigger setting usable (travel calibration, top and bottom dead zones, separate press and release sensitivity), set in a browser driver with no install, and a named reviewer saw it run at or near 8 kHz over USB. The mechanism separates Hall effect boards from ordinary mechanical ones; it does not separate the NS68 from the MCHOSE Ace 60 Pro, Epomaker HE68 Lite or Redragon K617 HE, whose pages I could not open. Whether the $39.99 Tri-mode NS68 keeps 8K on 2.4 GHz is unread, so the page should say the 8 kHz observation is for the Wired version.

findings.label: What rapid trigger is, in a maker's words
findings.value: Wooting: "dynamically activating and deactivating the key based on travel distance instead of a fixed point"; Wooting says it can be set "as sensitive as 0.1mm"
findings.note: Wooting originated the feature. The page does not explain the Hall sensor, dead zones or calibration.

findings.label: Rapid trigger sensitivity range
findings.value: 0.01 mm to 2 mm, with press and release sensitivity set separately
findings.source_title: Gamakay x NaughShark NS68 review, TechXReviews (Moussa Obscur, 2025-05-08)
findings.note: Reviewer's description of the driver settings, not a measurement of real sensor resolution. Wired variant reviewed.

findings.label: Dead zones
findings.value: Top and bottom dead zones adjustable, down to 0.0 mm ("Zero Deadzone")
findings.source_title: Gamakay x NaughShark NS68 review, TechXReviews (Moussa Obscur, 2025-05-08)
findings.note: A setting in the driver as the reviewer described it; not tested for false triggers at 0.0 mm.

findings.label: Calibration and software
findings.value: Travel calibration routine in a web-based driver at qmk.top; Music Follow and Light Shadow lighting modes need a separate downloadable driver
findings.source_title: Gamakay x NaughShark NS68 review, TechXReviews (Moussa Obscur, 2025-05-08)
findings.note: Reviewer's account from May 2025. I did not open the driver site.

findings.label: Polling rate observed over USB
findings.value: At or very close to 8,000 Hz in Keyboard Inspector; the web driver does not let you change it
findings.source_title: Gamakay x NaughShark NS68 review, TechXReviews (Moussa Obscur, 2025-05-08)
findings.note: Moussa Obscur's software check on the Wired version. The review gives nothing for 2.4 GHz or Bluetooth, and the Tri-mode was out of stock when the review was made. It also reports a 32 kHz scan rate, which differs from the 16K scan rate in our NS75 record; that is a different model.

findings.label: Switches and hot-swap
findings.value: Outemu Peach linear magnetic switches fitted; hot-swappable with 3-pin magnetic switches, Gateron and TTC named as compatible
findings.source_title: Gamakay x NaughShark NS68 review, TechXReviews (Moussa Obscur, 2025-05-08)
findings.note: Reviewer's statement. Switch travel is not given.

findings.label: Rival coverage: calibration and switch swaps
findings.value: mechanicalkeyboard.net: "magnet position, polarity and firmware calibration relevant when swapping switches"; "Even if a replacement physically fits, it can behave poorly unless the board supports it."
findings.source_title: Best Budget Hall Effect Keyboards Under $100 (2026)
findings.note: Last updated 2026-11-10. Does not discuss dead zones, 0.01 mm versus sensor resolution, or temperature drift. Does not pick the NS68.

findings.label: Rival coverage: recalibration fixes double registration
findings.value: gamepadsquire.com reports double-registration in specific games, "usually resolved by recalibrating the board"; also says "there is no web-based configurator"
findings.source_title: Best Budget Hall Effect Keyboards Under $100 in 2026
findings.note: Updated 2026-08-09. A rival page's claim, not a maker statement.

findings.label: Rival coverage: 8K is wired-only
findings.value: gamepadsquire.com: "The 2.4GHz mode tops out at 1,000Hz — the 8K figure is wired-only"
findings.source_title: Best Budget Hall Effect Keyboards Under $100 in 2026
findings.note: Shows rivals already cover the connection-mode limit for at least one budget board.

findings.label: Rival coverage: rapid trigger definition
findings.value: setupinsider.com: "Rapid trigger resets a key the moment you start lifting it, instead of waiting for it to pass a fixed point."; keyboardverdict.com: the board "resets the actuation point dynamically, the instant you start letting go of the key"
findings.source_title: Best Budget Gaming Keyboard Under $100 (2026): Rapid Trigger for $40
findings.note: The second quote is from https://www.keyboardverdict.com/best/best-rapid-trigger-keyboard/ (dated 2026-10-03), read the same day. Neither page covers dead zones or calibration, and keyboardverdict does not mention the NS68.
